inputs.query: I am on a week to week lease and I am one day late on rent, I just got a 72 hour eviction notice. dont I get 5 day buffer for late rent?

facts: Tenant is on a week-to-week lease.
Tenant is one day late on rent.
Landlord served Tenant with a 72-hour eviction notice for the late rent.
Question pertains to ORS 90.394 and ORS 90.160

ORS 90.394(1): "When the tenancy is a week-to-week tenancy, by delivering to the tenant at least 72 hours' written notice of nonpayment and the landlord's intention to terminate the rental agreement if the rent is not paid within that period. The landlord shall give this notice no sooner than on the fifth day of the rental period, including the first day the rent is due."
ORS 90.395(2): "A landlord shall deliver a copy of the notice posted on the website of the Judicial Department under ORS 105.136 along with: (a) Any notice of termination for nonpayment..."

ORS 90.395(3)(a): A court shall dismiss a complaint for possession based on a nonpayment termination notice if "the landlord failed to deliver the notice as required under subsection (2) of this section."

reference_conversation.content: I am on a week to week lease and I am one day late on rent, I just got a 72 hour eviction notice. dont I get 5 day buffer for late rent?

Under [ORS 90.394](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.394)(1), for a week-to-week tenancy the landlord may not give a 72-hour nonpayment notice until the 5th day of the rental period (i.e., after rent is at least five days late). Because you got the notice only one day after rent was due, it's premature and legally defective.

Also check whether the notice included the required rental assistance information. Under [ORS 90.395](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.395)(2), a landlord must deliver a copy of the Judicial Department's rental assistance notice alongside any nonpayment termination notice. If they didn't, that's a separate defect - a court must dismiss the eviction complaint under [ORS 90.395](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.395)(3)(a).

Put the landlord on notice in writing that the notice is invalid, and pay the rent immediately if you can.

inputs.query: If ive moved out but there are some things I forgot, can my landlord throw them away?

facts: Tenant moved out but left personal belongings behind.
Questions pertains to ORS 90.425

ORS 90.155(1): "Except as provided in ORS 90.300, 90.315, 90.425 and 90.675, where this chapter requires written notice, service or delivery of that written notice shall be executed by one or more of the following methods..." (ORS 90.425 is explicitly excluded from ORS 90.155; it has its own service rules - there is no 'post' or attachment option for abandoned property notices.)

ORS 90.425(3): Prior to storing, selling or disposing of the tenant's personal property, the landlord must give a written notice to the tenant that must be: (a) Personally delivered to the tenant; or (b) Sent by first class mail addressed and mailed to the tenant. There is no option to post or attach the notice.

ORS 90.425(6)(b): For all abandoned personal property other than manufactured dwellings or floating homes, the tenant must contact the landlord "not less than five days after personal delivery or eight days after mailing of the notice." Both windows must be stated - the 5-day window applies to personal delivery, the 8-day window applies only to mailed notice.

ORS 90.425(8): After the tenant responds, "the landlord must make that personal property available for removal by the tenant...by appointment at reasonable times during the 15 days...following the date of the response." This 15-day window begins after the tenant contacts the landlord; it is separate from and subsequent to the contact deadline.

ORS 90.425(7)(d): The landlord "is entitled to reasonable or actual storage charges and costs incidental to storage or disposal, including any cost of removal to a place of storage." ORS 90.425(8): For property abandoned under subsection (2)(a) or (b) (but not (2)(c)), the landlord may require payment of removal and storage charges before releasing the property to the tenant. Stating that the tenant may owe removal and storage costs is legally correct - it is not an overstatement of landlord rights.

reference_conversation.content: If ive moved out but there are some things I forgot, can my landlord throw them away?

Not right away. Under [ORS 90.425](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.425) your ex-landlord must:
1. Give you written notice (personally delivered or sent by first-class mail - there is no option to post or attach the notice, because [ORS 90.155](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.155) explicitly excludes ORS 90.425 from its general service rules). The notice must list the items, where they're stored, and a deadline to contact the landlord.
2. Give you enough time to respond: at least 5 days from personal delivery, or at least 8 days from mailing ([ORS 90.425](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.425)(6)(b)).
3. Once you contact the landlord by that deadline, make the property available for pickup for 15 days after your response, by appointment at reasonable times ([ORS 90.425](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.425)(8)).
4. Note that if your property was abandoned under typical circumstances (you left without notice), the landlord may require you to pay reasonable removal and storage costs before releasing your belongings, under [ORS 90.425](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.425)(7)(d) and (8).
Only after those deadlines pass can the landlord sell, donate, or dispose of what's left. If the landlord skips these steps you can sue for up to twice your actual losses (at least one month's rent).

inputs.query: I have a month to month tenancy and am trying to give 30 days notice but my landlord is saying that isn't enough warning

Landlord claims 30 days notice is insufficient..
Tenant has not yet confirmed whether the notice was written, dated, and properly delivered.

ORS 90.427(3)(a): "At any time during the tenancy, the tenant may terminate the tenancy by giving the landlord notice in writing not less than 30 days prior to the date designated in the notice for the termination of the tenancy."

ORS 90.245(1): "A rental agreement may not provide that the tenant: (a) Agrees to waive or forgo rights or remedies under this chapter..." ORS 90.245(2): "A provision prohibited by subsection (1) of this section included in a rental agreement is unenforceable."

reference_conversation.content: I have a month to month tenancy and am trying to give 30 days notice but my landlord is saying that isn't enough warning

In Oregon a month-to-month renter may end the tenancy 'by giving the landlord notice in writing not less than 30 days prior to the date designated in the notice for the termination of the tenancy.' (ORS 90.427 (3)(a) or, for MH/floating-home spaces, ORS 90.620 (1).)
Tips to avoid push-back:
* Put the notice in writing and date it.
* Specify your last day of possession.
* Serve it by personal delivery or by first-class mail (add three days if mailed) (ORS 90.155, 90.160).
If you do those things, 30 days is all the statute requires; the landlord cannot insist on more.

inputs.query: If my landlord put my security deposit in an interest-bearing account, are they required to give me the interest when I move out?

PCC 30.01.087(B)(1): "Within two weeks following receipt of a tenant's funds paid as a security deposit or for last-month's rent, a landlord must deposit all of such funds into a secure financial institution account segregated from the landlord's personal and business operating accounts. If the account is an interest-bearing account, all interest will accrue proportionately to the benefit of the tenant and must be returned to the tenant with the unused security deposit in accordance with Subsection B.2. below. If the account bears interest, the landlord is required to pay such interest in full, minus an optional five percent deduction for administrative costs from such interest, to the tenant unless it is used to cover any claims for damage. For interest bearing accounts, the landlord must provide a receipt of the account and any interest earned at the tenant's request, no more than once per year. reference_conversation.content: If my landlord put my security deposit in an interest-bearing account, are they required to give me the interest when I move out?

Yes. In Portland, if your landlord puts your security deposit in an interest-bearing account, the interest accrues to you. The landlord must return the interest with your deposit, though they can deduct up to 5% of the interest for administrative costs.

According to Portland City Code 30.01.087(B), your rental agreement must state the name and address of the bank where the deposit is held and whether the account is interest-bearing.

Does your written rental agreement mention an interest-bearing account?

inputs.query: I have a three year lease that started in November 2025. I am trying to break it. Is a three year lease enforceable?

facts: Tenant has a fixed-term lease.
Fixed-term lease is three years.
Tenant wants to break the lease.

ORS 90.100(19): "'Fixed term tenancy' means a tenancy that has a fixed term of existence, continuing to a specific ending date and terminating on that date without requiring further notice to effect the termination."
Oregon law does not cap residential lease length - a three-year lease is generally enforceable as a binding contract.

ORS 90.410(3): "If the tenant abandons the dwelling unit, the landlord shall make reasonable efforts to rent it for a fair rental. If the landlord rents the dwelling unit for a term beginning before the expiration of the rental agreement, the rental agreement terminates as of the date of the new tenancy. If the landlord fails to use reasonable efforts to rent the dwelling unit at a fair rental or if the landlord accepts the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is deemed to be terminated by the landlord as of the date the landlord knows or should know of the abandonment."

ORS 90.302(2)(e): "The abandonment or relinquishment of a dwelling unit during a fixed term tenancy without cause. The fee may not exceed one and one-half times the monthly rent." And ORS 90.302(2)(e)(C): "ORS 90.410(3) does not apply to the abandonment or relinquishment" - meaning if this fee is charged, the mitigation duty is replaced by the flat fee cap.

reference_conversation.content: I have a three year lease that started in November 2025. I am trying to break it. Is a three year lease enforceable?

Yes, a three-year lease is generally enforceable in Oregon - there is no law that limits residential lease length. It is a binding fixed-term tenancy under [ORS 90.100(19)](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.100).

If you break it, two scenarios apply depending on your lease:

1. **No early-termination clause**: The landlord must try to re-rent the unit (duty to mitigate damages under [ORS 90.410(3)](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.410)). You owe rent only until a new tenant moves in, plus the landlord's reasonable re-letting costs.
2. **Early-termination fee in the lease**: Under [ORS 90.302(2)(e)](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.302), the landlord may charge up to one and one-half times the monthly rent as a flat fee. If this applies, the mitigation rule in ORS 90.410 does not - your liability is capped at that fee.

Review your lease now for any early-termination or lease-break clause. Either way, notify your landlord in writing as soon as possible - giving them more lead time increases the chance they find a replacement tenant quickly, which limits what you owe.

inputs.query: my front door lock broke, how quickly does the landlord need to come fix it?

facts: Tenant's front door lock is broken.
Tenant wants to know how quickly the landlord must fix a broken front door lock.

ORS 90.320(1)(L): A dwelling unit is unhabitable if it substantially lacks "Working locks for all dwelling entrance doors, and, unless contrary to applicable law, latches for all windows, by which access may be had to that portion of the premises that the tenant is entitled under the rental agreement to occupy to the exclusion of others and keys for those locks that require keys."

ORS 90.100(15)(a)(A): 'Essential service' for a standard residential tenancy includes "Heat, plumbing, hot and cold running water, gas, electricity, light fixtures, locks for exterior doors, latches for windows and any cooking appliance or refrigerator supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord." - a broken exterior door lock is therefore an essential service.

ORS 90.365(1): "If contrary to the rental agreement or ORS 90.320 or 90.730 the landlord intentionally or negligently fails to supply any essential service, the tenant may give written notice to the landlord specifying the breach and that the tenant may seek substitute services, diminution in rent damages or substitute housing. After allowing the landlord a reasonable time and reasonable access under the circumstances to supply the essential service, the tenant may: (a) Procure reasonable amounts of the essential service during the period of the landlord's noncompliance and deduct their actual and reasonable cost from the rent; (b) Recover damages based upon the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit; or (c) If the failure to supply an essential service makes the dwelling unit unsafe or unfit to occupy, procure substitute housing during the period of the landlord's noncompliance, in which case the tenant is excused from paying rent for the period of the landlord's noncompliance."
ORS 90.365 does not define 'reasonable time' - it depends on the circumstances. A broken exterior lock is an urgent safety matter and a very short response time is expected.
Portland has no local ordinance that sets a specific deadline for lock repairs.
Before pursuing remedies under ORS 90.365, the tenant must first give the landlord written notice specifying the breach.

reference_conversation.content: my front door lock broke, how quickly does the landlord need to come fix it?

A broken front door lock is a habitability issue and an essential service your landlord must fix promptly.

Under [ORS 90.320(1)(l)](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.320), landlords must maintain working locks on all dwelling entrance doors. A functioning exterior lock is also an 'essential service' under [ORS 90.100(15)(a)(A)](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.100).

The first step is to notify your landlord in writing that the lock is broken. Once you've done that and allowed a reasonable time for them to respond, [ORS 90.365(1)](https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_90.365) gives you several options if the landlord fails to act:
- Have the lock repaired yourself and deduct the actual, reasonable cost from your rent.
- Recover damages for the reduced rental value of your unit while the lock is broken.
- If the broken lock makes the unit unsafe or unfit to occupy, find substitute housing and be excused from paying rent during that period.

What 'reasonable time' means depends on the circumstances - for an exterior lock it is a safety matter, so the expected response is very short. Portland has no local rule that sets a more specific deadline.

Have you given your landlord written notice yet?

inputs.query: I accidentally missed my first court appearance for an eviction, I don't think my landlord has a good case, will the court consider both sides or only rule for him because he's there?

facts: Tenant accidentally missed their first court appearance for an eviction.
Tenant believes the landlord does not have a strong case.
Tenant has not yet called the court clerk but is about to.
Question pertains to ORS 105.137.
ORS 105.137 says that a court may enter a default judgment giving the landlord possession and awarding court costs when the tenant does not show up for the first hearing in an eviction case

reference_conversation.content: I accidentally missed my first court appearance for an eviction, I don't think my landlord has a good case, will the court consider both sides or only rule for him because he's there?

In Oregon eviction cases, if the tenant does not appear at the first court date, the landlord will probably win automatically because the judge normally enters a default judgment giving the landlord possession when the tenant does not show up (ORS 105.137). The court does not weigh the landlord's evidence or consider your side of the case unless you are there to argue your side. This means you could be at risk of being locked out of your home, and should take action immediately. Deadlines are tight, so act TODAY. Here's what you can still do: 1. Call the court clerk (look for their phone number in the papers you received about your eviction case) and ask: --> Has the judge already **entered a default judgment** in my eviction case? (i.e., did the court rule against you?) --> Has a **writ of restitution** issued yet? (i.e., has the court issued papers to have you locked-out?) 2. If the court has not yet entered judgment, ask the clerk whether you can file an Answer and request a new trial date. The Answer is a official legal document that states the reasons why you should win the case (your "legal defenses"). 3. If the case has already been decided (i.e., judgment has already been entered), you may file a motion to set aside default judgment as soon as possible (as soon as possible and definitely before the sheriff actually begins the lock-out process by posting a writ). Explain you missed the appearance by mistake and state any defenses you have (for example, the termination notice was defective under ORS 90.394 for listing a wrong amount of rent owed or wrong dates, the landlord did not properly provide the notice of termination to you as required under ORS 90.155, the notice was served in retaliation under ORS 90.385, or other reasons). Bring copies of any defective notice or proof of rent payments when you file the motion. To connect with an attorney for further assistance with completing and filing an Answer, Motion to Set Aside a Defaulat Judgment, or other support, see **REFERRAL PAGE**

It was good that you notified the landlord about the problem, but you may need to take further action to make this notice official and pursue other remedies. inputs.query: I received an eviction notice and within the time I was able to pay half the funds, now what?

facts: Tenant received an eviction notice for non-payment of rent.
Tenant was able to pay only half of the rent amount within the notice period.
Tenant has not shared whether Landlord accepted the half-payment.
Question pertains to ORS 90.417 and ORS 90.394

ORS 90.417 says that if a landlord accepts a partial rent payment for a month, they cannot evict a tenant for nonpayment of rent unless the payment was made as part of a written payment plan and was not made in the amount or within the time provided by such plan, or the tenant and landlord signed a written agreement after the payment was made stating that acceptance of the payment does not waive the landlord's claim to the full rent amount
ORS 90.394 says that a notice of termination for nonpayment of rent may be cured by the tenant by paying the full amount stated in the notice by the deadline stated in the notice

reference_conversation.content: I received an eviction notice and within the time I was able to pay half the funds, now what?

It depends on (1) whether the landlord accepted the rent payment (kept or deposited it), (2) whether the payment was made as part of a written payment plan, and (3) whether you and your landlord signed an agreement after the payment was made stating that acceptance of the payment does not waive the landlord's claim to the full rent amount. Here is how each factor could impact your situation: 1. If your landlord accepted the partial rent payment, they probably cannot evict you for not paying that month's rent (ORS 90.417(4)). A landlord is not required to accept a partial rent payment, however, so keep an eye out for any notices or messages from your landlord stating that they are choosing not to accept your payment. 2. If the payment was made as part of the written payment plan, then your landlord can only evict you if the payment was not made in the amount or at the time required by that plan (ORS 90.417(4)(a)). 3. If you and your landlord signed a written agreement after the payment was made stating that acceptance of the payment does not waive the landlord's claim to the full rent amount, then you can still be evicted for not having paid rent even though you made the partial payment (ORS 90.417(4)(b)). In any event, make sure you keep proof (receipt, copy of check or online payment) that the landlord accepted any payment from you. If the landlord serves a NEW notice for nonpayment of rent based on the same month, or files a eviction lawsuit based on the existing notice, you can may be able to raise the landlord's acceptance of payment as a legal defense (i.e., a legal reason why the case shouldn't be allowed to move forward). Of course, an eviction notice for non-payment of rent can also be resolved ("cured") by paying the FULL amount stated in the notice by the deadline stated in the notice (ORS 90.394). Has your landlord accepted the partial rent payment you made? If so, did you sign any additional agreement relating to it?

inputs.query: I am 5 days late on my rent and I was given a 10 day eviction notice, what should I do?

Landlord served Tenant with a 10-day non-payment eviction notice on the 5th day of the rent period.
The notice lists a termination date of the 15th.
Question pertains to ORS 90.394

ORS 90.394 says that a landlord may serve 10-day notice of termination for nonpayment of rent only if it is served on or after the eighth day of the rental period, and that a notice of termination for nonpayment of rent that is served on or after fifth day of the rental period but before the eighth day must be 13-day notice

reference_conversation.content: I am 5 days late on my rent and I was given a 10 day eviction notice, what should I do?

You may be able to challenge the validity of the notice based on when it was delivered to you. State law (ORS 90.394(2)(a)) allows a 10-day non-payment notice only if it's served on or after the 8th day of the rent period. If a notice for nonpayment of rent is served on or after 5th day of the rental period but before the 8th day, state law (ORS 90.394(2)(b)) says that it needs to be 13-day notice instead. Additionally, a notice for nonpayment of rent may be invalid if it fails to state the exact amount you must pay to resolve ("cure") the notice or if it fails to state the date on which your tenancy will be terminated (i.e., when you will lose the legal right to reside in the property), so be sure to check the notice for those details as well. At any rate, you should take action immediately to respond to the notice because the landlord may file an eviction lawsuit against you if you do not respond. If you can pay the past-due rent, submit payment to the landlord as soon as possible and no later than any date listed on the notice to cure the notice. If you want to challenge the vailidity of the notice of nonpayment, write a letter to your landlord (and keep a copy of the letter) pointing out the defect and reiterating that you remain willing to pay. If the landlord files an eviction lawsuit based on this notice, make sure to raise the invalidity of the notice under ORS 90.394(2) as a defense. Would you like me to assist you in drafting a letter to your landlord challenging the validity of the notice?

reference_conversation.content: My dog bit my neighbor and he called my landlord. Now my landlord is threatening to evict me -- can he do that?

Under Oregon law, (ORS 90.396(1)(a)) a landlord may evict a tenant if a pet causes inflicts or threatens to inflict substantial personal injury to another person on the premises. However, the landlord must give a 24-hour termination notice that states (i) what happened (the bite), (ii) the exact date and time that your tenancy will end, and (iii) that you can stop the eviction by permanently removing the dog before that deadline (ORS 90.396(2)). If your landlord has not given you a written notice of termination, or the notice does not state all three pieces of information listed above, you may be able block the eviction and/or give yourself more time to resolve the situation by challenging the legal validity of the notice. inputs.query: My landlord is in foreclosure and the bank used my security deposit to cover what the landlord owes, does that mean I've paid my rent for the month?

facts: Tenant's landlord is in foreclosure.
Bank took Tenant's security deposit to satisfy landlord's debt.
Tenant has not yet given written notice to apply the deposit to rent.
Tenant has received written notice that the property is in foreclosure.
Tenant is considering applying the security deposit to this month's rent.
Question pertains to ORS 90.300 and ORS 90.367
ORS 90.367 says that a security deposit or prepaid rent in the landlord's possession is not garnishable property
ORS 90.300 says that a tenant may apply their security deposit or prepaid rent to their rent obligations, but only if the tenant gives the landlord written notice that the tenant is doing so

reference_conversation.content: My landlord is in foreclosure and the bank used my security deposit to cover what the landlord owes, does that mean I've paid my rent for the month?

No, your rent is not automatically paid just because the bank took your security deposit. A security deposit or prepaid rent in the landlord's possession is not garnishable property (ORS 90.300(17)(a)), so it should not have been seized to satisfy your landlord's debt in the first place. You do, however, have your own right to use that money for rent. Because you have received actual notice that the property is in foreclosure, (ORS 90.367(1)) lets you apply your security deposit or prepaid rent to your rent obligation -- but only if you give your landlord written notice that you are doing so. A few important points: --> The written notice is what makes the credit effective. Without it, this month's rent is still legally owed and your landlord can serve you a termination notice for nonpayment of rent. --> If you have already received a notice of termination for nonpayment of rent, you can still deliver a written notice within the cure period stated in that notice (ORS 90.367(3)) to apply the security deposit to the missed month's rent. --> Applying the deposit does not end your tenancy, and your landlord may not terminate you for applying it (ORS 90.367(2)). --> If your landlord later shares written evidence (such as a letter from a lender) that the property is no longer in foreclosure, they can require you to restore the deposit, and must allow you at least two months to do it (ORS 90.367(5)). Because the bank took the money rather than you electing to apply it, you should put your election in writing so there is no dispute later about whether rent was paid. Would you like me to help you draft the written notice applying your deposit to this month's rent?

inputs.query: I've been evicted, what happens now with the rent I owed? The judgment included $4,000 in unpaid rent and I had paid a $1,200 security deposit.

facts: Tenant was evicted and owes $4,000 in unpaid rent per the eviction judgment.
Tenant's security deposit (and any prepaid rent) was $1,200.
Landlord has not yet provided a written accounting or refund of the deposit.
Tenant gave the landlord a forwarding address.
Question pertains to ORS 90.300

ORS 90.300 says that within 31 days after a tenancy terminates and the tenant delivers possession, the landlord must apply the security deposit and any prepaid rent to any rent the tenant still owes and mail the tenant a written accounting that itemizes each deduction and explains the reason for it, along with any refund still owed

reference_conversation.content: I've been evicted, what happens now with the rent I owed? The judgment included $4,000 in unpaid rent and I had paid a $1,200 security deposit.

You remain liable (i.e., you legally must pay) for rent that accrued up to the date the landlord regained possession, and because a court entered a money judgment, that $4,000 can be collected like any other civil judgment through wage or bank garnishment (which is a a deduction from your paycheck). Your $1,200 deposit still has to be accounted for, though, which may allow you to recover some money. Under (ORS 90.300(12)) and (ORS 90.300(13)), within 31 days after the tenancy terminates and you deliver possession (i.e., when you return the keys), your landlord must: --> Apply your security deposit and any prepaid rent to what you actually owe; and --> Mail you a written accounting that itemizes each deduction and explains the reason for it, along with any refund still owed (by check or by e-deposit if you signed an agreement with the landlord to process payments electronically). If your landlord withholds the deposit without that written accounting, or withholds it in bad faith, you can recover twice the amount wrongfully withheld (ORS 90.300(16)). Tenant is unsure whether the notice may be discriminatory.
Question pertains to ORS 90.427, ORS 90.155, ORS 90.160, PCC 30.01.085, and EC 8.425
ORS 90.155 lists acceptable methods of service of notice and that if the notice is mailed, three days should be added to the period provided by the notice
ORS 90.160 says that days are counted the day the notice was served but including the last day
PCC 30.01.085 requires at least 90 days' notice for a no-cause termination plus relocation assistance of $2,900 to $4,500 depending on unit size, subject to certain exemptions
EC 8.425 requires relocation assistance equal to two months' rent for a no-cause termination with some exemptions
ORS 90.427 says that a landlord end a month-to-month tenancy within the first year without cause by giving written notice at least 30 days before the termination date stated in the notice

reference_conversation.content: I moved in eight months ago and I am on a month to month lease. My landlord is trying to give me a 30 day no-cause eviction, is that really enough time?

For a month-to-month tenancy, 30 days' notice is legally sufficient during the first year of occupancy. State law, (ORS 90.427(3)(b)), lets a landlord end a month-to-month tenancy within the first year for no reason ("without cause") by giving written notice at least 30 days before the termination date stated in the notice. After the first year, the landlord would generally need to provide at least 90 days' notice and a qualifying reason, i.e., a "cause" for eviction (unless the landlord also occupies the building as a primary residence and it has no more than two dwelling units, in which case shorter notice may be appropriate, see (ORS 90.427(8))). Even in the first year, the notice is valid only if: --> It is in writing and states the exact date the tenancy terminates. --> It was served in one of the ways allowed by (ORS 90.155). Important note: if the notice was mailed, three days should be added to the period provided by the notice. --> The termination date is at least 30 consecutive calendar days out, counted without the day the notice was served but including the last day (ORS 90.160(1)). --> The notice has not been served in retaliation for asserting a tenant right (ORS 90.385) nor served in discrimination of a protected personal characteristic, including your race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, familial status, disability status, or source of income (ORS 90.390). If the notice was served for either of those reasons, you can raise that as a defense to an eviction based on the notice. Where you live also matters, because certain local laws require longer notice. In Portland, (PCC 30.01.085) requires at least 90 days' notice for a no-cause termination plus relocation assistance of $2,900 to $4,500 depending on unit size, subject to listed exemptions. In Eugene, (EC 8.425) requires relocation assistance equal to two months' rent for a no-cause termination, also with exemptions. What city is your rental in, and what date was the notice served on you?

reference_conversation.content: I have lived in my apartment for four years and 15 days ago my landlord gave me a 90-day notice that the property will be demolished. Is this legal, and if so, does my landlord have to pay me to move out?

A landlord can use a 90-day notice to end a month-to-month tenancy in order to demolish the unit or convert it to a non-residential use, but only by following (ORS 90.427(5)(a)) and (ORS 90.427(6)) exactly. On the facts you describe, the notice may be defective. The notice is only legal if all of these are true: --> It is in writing, gives at least 90 days, and states the date the tenancy terminates. --> It states that the unit will be demolished or converted, and presents facts supporting that the landlord truly intends to do so. --> At the time the notice was delivered, the landlord paid you an amount equal to one month's rent as a relocation payment (ORS 90.427(6)(a)(C)). That payment is due when the notice is handed to you, not later. The only exception is a landlord who has an ownership interest in four or fewer residential dwelling units (ORS 90.427(6)(b)). If your landlord owns more than four, the missing payment makes the notice invalid. Notify your landlord in writing (and keep a copy of the letter) that you believe the notice is invalid and that you are entitled to relocation assistance. Unless and until the landlord serves a new notice that meets all of the requirements listed above, you do not have to move, and you should keep paying rent as usual. If the landlord files for eviction anyway, you can raise the notice defect is a legal defense (i.e., reason why you should win the case), and you may recover an amount equal to three months' rent plus your actual damages (ORS 90.427(9)(a)). If your unit is in Portland, (PCC 30.01.085) separately requires relocation assistance of $2,900 to $4,500 paid at least 45 days before the termination date. Possibly, but repairs are the narrowest of the qualifying landlord reasons, and notices based on them are often defective. Under (ORS 90.427(5)(b)), a landlord may end a month-to-month tenancy after the first year in order to undertake repairs or renovations only if the premises are already unsafe or unfit for occupancy, or will be unsafe or unfit while the work is done, and the landlord must state facts in the notice to support this. Ordinary maintenance, upgrades, or work you could reasonably live through does not qualify. The 90-day notice must also (under (ORS 90.427(6)(a))): --> Be in writing and state the date the tenancy terminates; --> Specify the qualifying reason for the eviction and the facts supporting it, including the repair being made (as explained above); and --> Be delivered together with a payment equal to one month's periodic rent, unless the landlord has an ownership interest in four or fewer residential dwelling units (ORS 90.427(6)(b)). If any of those pieces is missing, the notice is not valid and the landlord cannot file an eviction case based on it. If your landlord does file an eviction lawsuit based on this notice, you can raise the defect as a defense (i.e., a legal reason why you should win the case) and you may be able to recover three months' rent plus actual damages (ORS 90.427(9)(a)). reference_conversation.content: My landlord wants to evict me out of the other half of the duplex she lives in so her uncle can move in, can she do that? I have lived there for for a little over a year and although I signed a lease when I moved in, I am now renting month to month.

Evictions for no reason ("no cause" evictions) are limited in Oregon, but are allowed where a tenant lives in the same building as their landlord's primary residence and the building contains no more than two dwelling units (ORS 90.427(8)). After the first year of occupancy, a landlord in that situation may end a month-to-month tenancy for any reason ("without cause") by giving written notice not less than 60 days before the date of termination (ORS 90.427(8)(a)(B)). So, your landlord probably can evict you without giving a reason for doing so. Her uncle moving in does not change the analysis, and, unfortunately, no relocation payment is required in this circumstance. However, your landlord still needs to give you a written notice that meets all requirements under state law. Specifically, the notice must: --> Be in writing and state the exact date the tenancy terminates. --> Be served in one of the ways allowed by (ORS 90.155), and if it is mailed, include three additional days in the notice period. --> Provide no less than 60 days (plus three additional days if the notice is served by mail), counted in consecutive calendar days, not counting the day of service but including the last day (ORS 90.160(1)). --> Not be served retaliation for asserting a tenant right (ORS 90.385) nor served in discrimination of a protected personal characteristic, including your race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, marital status, familial status, disability status, or source of income (ORS 90.390). If the notice was served for either of those reasons, you can raise that as a defense to an eviction based on the notice. Note that city law may require more than the 60 days mandated by state law. If your duplex is in Portland, (PCC 30.01.085) requires at least 90 days' written notice for a no-cause termination. If it is in Eugene, (EC 8.425) you may be entitled to a relocation payment of two months' rent if the landlord has occupied her unit as a principal residence for less than six months. If the notice gives fewer than the required days, leaves out the termination date, or was served improperly, it is invalid and you can stay until she serves a proper notice and obtains a court judgment. She cannot legally change the locks, remove your belongings, or shut off utilities to force you out. Question pertains to ORS 90.427
ORS 90.427 only allows a tenancy to be terminated for certain causes, and the sale of a property is not an acceptable cause to end a tenancy

reference_conversation.content: I rent a condo owned by somebody who does not own the building, just the unit, and they want to sell it, do I have any rights? I am on my second one-year lease with 5 months left.

Yes, you do have rights as a tenant -- the owner selling the condo does not end your lease. Under (ORS 90.427(4)(a)), a landlord may terminate a fixed term tenancy during the term only for certain reasons ("causes"). The sale of a property is not an acceptable cause to end a tenancy, so your lease runs to its stated end date, and whoever buys the unit simply steps into your current landlord's place and is bound by every term -- the rent, the rules, and the remaining five months. There are only a couple of scenarios in which your landlord could force you to move out sooner: --> You violate the rental agreement or otherwise do something that creates a cause for eviction, and the landlord (current or new) serves a valid for-cause termination notice under (ORS 90.392) or (ORS 90.396). This could happen if you were to, for example, cause damage to the property or harm another tenant. --> You voluntarily sign an early move-out or cash-for-keys agreement. This would be a negotiation -- you are not required to sign anything, and you should not sign until you understand what you are giving up and feel like you are getting a good deal. When your fixed-term lease expires, it becomes a month-to-month tenancy unless you agree to a new fixed term, you give written notice at least 30 days before the term ends that you are leaving, or the landlord has a qualifying reason and gives proper notice (ORS 90.427(4)ORS 90.427(4)(c)). That third scenario is how the sale can eventually end your tenancy: the owner may serve a written 90-day notice with a termination date no earlier than the end of your fixed-term lease IF they have accepting an offer to purchase from a buyer who intends in good faith to occupy the unit as a primary residence. The termination notice from your landlord must include written evidence of the offer, plus a relocation payment equal to one month's rent delivered with the notice, unless the landlord has an ownership interest in four or fewer residential dwelling units (ORS 90.427(5)--(6)). Has your landlord given you any official notices or requested to negotiate an early move-out agreement? Any notice you receive before your lease ends that gives only the sale as the reason is invalid. Has the owner asked you to sign anything or given you written notice to move?

reference_conversation.content: My son attacked me and a neighbor who tried to help, now we received a 24 hour eviction notice, is that legal? He is 20 and also on the lease.

Based on the facts you describe, 24-hour notice is probably legal for your son. It is probably not legal/effective to evict you. State law, (ORS 90.396(1)(a)), allows a landlord to terminate a tenancy with 24 hours' written notice when a tenant inflicts substantial personal injury on a person on the premises other than the tenant, so the assault itself is a lawful basis for a 24-hour notice against your son. However, where the perpetrator and the victim are both tenants of the same household, state law ((ORS 90.445(1)(a))) says that the landlord may terminate the rental agreement of the perpetrating tenant, "but may not terminate the rental agreement of the other tenants." If your son stays past the termination date and time in the notice, the landlord's remedy is a court order removing him alone, without seeking possession from you (ORS 90.445(1)(b)). (ORS 90.449(1)(b)) reinforces this and provides legal protections for you if the landlord does try to evict you. That statute says that a landlord may not terminate a tenancy, or serve a notice to terminate, because of a violation that consists of an incident of domestic violence committed against the tenant. So, a 24-hour notice that lists you as a terminated tenant is defective as to you, and if the landlord acts on it you can raise that as a defense to eviction and recover damages of up to two months’ rent (ORS 90.449(4)). What to do now: --> Send your landlord a dated letter (keep a copy) stating that you and the neighbor were the victims, that ORS 90.445(1)(a) permits terminating only the perpetrator's tenancy, and that the notice is void as to you. --> Gather documentation showing you were the victim, such as the police report number or a restraining order. Based on the facts you have shared, your landlord can probably only evict your boyfriend and not you. Under (ORS 90.445(1)(a)), when a tenant commits a criminal act of physical violence related to domestic violence against a household member who is also a tenant, the landlord may terminate the perpetrator's rental agreement on 24 hours' written notice but "may not terminate the rental agreement of the other tenants." If your landlord takes any of the actions listed above, you may be be entitled to recover damages (i.e., money to address the landlord's violation of law), assert it as a legal defense (a reason why you should win the case) in an eviction lawsuit, and/or seek an order from the court requiring the landlord to follow the law (ORS 90.449(4)). To ensure you can effectively assert these protections, you should take a few practical steps.
